The AM1 alloy is a first-generation monocrystalline nickel-based superalloy used for high-pressure turbine blades in aeronautical gas turbines.
Previous studies on the oxidation of AM1 and similar superalloys have only reported data at the highest temperatures of use (1100-1150°C).
The SMT-TGA method was used to measure the oxidation kinetics of AM1 over the wide temperature range of 750-1300°C using a single sample.
Over the temperature range of 1050-1300°C, the parabolic rate constant (kp) for AM1 followed a single Arrhenius law close to that reported for the growth of α-alumina on NiAl.
Between 750-950°C, the kp values for AM1 followed a different Arrhenius law, indicating a transient oxidation regime.
The transient oxidation regime was characterized by a decrease in kp over time, especially pronounced at the lower temperatures.
Isothermal oxidation tests confirmed the transient oxidation behavior of AM1, showing a fast initial oxidation rate followed by a slower parabolic regime.
XRD and SEM-EBSD analysis showed the oxide scale on AM1 at 1100°C was composed of α-alumina, spinel, and rutile precipitates.
At 950°C, the oxide scale contained α-alumina, spinel, rutile, bunsenite, and ilmenite, indicating a less protective scale.
At 800°C, alumina formed as elongated precipitates rather than a continuous protective layer.
The proposed model accounts for the initial fast growth of a transient mixed oxide followed by the gradual formation of a protective α-alumina layer.
The time required for AM1 to exit the transient oxidation regime and reach the steady-state parabolic kinetics can be determined using the proposed model.
The model allows predicting the oxidation kinetics of AM1 over the entire 750-1300°C temperature range studied.
Hafnium present in the AM1 alloy may contribute to the slightly lower parabolic rate constants compared to literature data for NiAl.
The SMT-TGA method proved effective for rapidly determining the oxidation kinetics of AM1 over a wide temperature range using a single sample.
